newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU proposes user-friendly phone plan.
newsitem.headline: EU proposes user-friendly phone plan.

text.p: Phone callers should be able to dial "388" from anywhere in Europe to order goods or reach a help line by the start of 1999, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
However, a proposal to set "3" as the common prefix for international calls to Europe needs more study, the European Union executive said in a package of proposals on phone numbering.

The Commission, seeking to bolster the EU's plan to open its telecommunications market to full competition next year, said subscribers should be able to keep their numbers when they switch phone companies by the start of 2000.

By that year, they should also be able to use their chosen phone company -- even if it is not the traditional monopoly -- for long-distance and international calls without having to dial an access code, it said.

"The availability of adequate numbers...allocated and designed on a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory basis, is an essential condition for effective competition, innovation and consumer choice," a Commission report said.
The Commission drew up its proposals after consulting telecoms operators, phone users, governments and others on a discussion paper that is issued last November.

It said there was broad agreement that the pan-European "388" code -- similar to the U.S.'s "800" or "900" numbers -- should be introduced by early 1999. The International Telecommunications Union is already in the process of clearing use of the code.

However, governments and telecoms operators were less keen about a Commission proposal to set "3" as a common "European country code", similar to the "1" used across the United States, a Commission telecoms official told reporters.
The official, Jean-Eric de Cockborne, said they argued that more study was needed into whether the benefits outweighed the costs of overhauling Europe's numbering system.

Existing EU laws require phone companies with "significant market power" to allow callers to select which carrier to use for long-distance or international calls on a call-by call basis by the start of 1998.
But the Commission said it would draw up new rules to ensure they can choose a carrier for such calls by default -- without having to dial a special code -- by the start of 2000.
It said it would study next year whether those rules should be extended to mobile phone operators.
EU rules also require companies to introduce "number portability", allowing callers to carry their phone numbers with them when they change servers or move -- by January 1, 2003.
However, following its consultations, the Commission will propose that the date be brought forward to January 1, 2000.

It said it would also push for common standards on "alphanumeric" dialling -- the layout of numbers and letters on a phone keyboard -- so that callers will be able to dial words rather than numbers, for example, "FLOWERS" to reach a florist.
